name: Dictatorship of the proletariat
summary: The dictatorship of the proletariat is the Marxist doctrine that, after the overthrow of the capitalist order, the working class must hold political power as a ruling class and use it to suppress the former exploiters, expropriate capital and reorganise society, until classes disappear and the state withers away. Marx and Engels meant a class rule on the model of the Paris Commune, with elected and recallable officials, an armed people and workmen's wages. Lenin added that it means suppression by force of the exploiters' resistance, democracy for the majority, Soviet power and, in his later texts, leadership by a disciplined party.
scope: The doctrine as the defining sources set it out (s1, s2): Marx and Engels from the Manifesto (1848) through the 1852 Weydemeyer letter, the Civil War in France with Engels's 1891 introduction (the Paris Commune named there as the dictatorship of the proletariat) and the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875), and Lenin's elaboration in The State and Revolution (1917), The Proletarian Revolution and the Renegade Kautsky (1918) and Left-Wing Communism (1920). All answers rest on these texts' words, not on the practice of any state; the regimes that claimed the doctrine (Marxism-Leninism in power) have their own entries and are not used here. Stalin's later codification and Maoist variants are excluded.
